description: Historical and contextual entities referenced by Books I–III. These records are separate from narrative presence: the local novel corpus supplies the trigger, while authoritative external sources supply concise historical context. first_section is a global spoiler threshold.

book2_exclusions.reason: Historical school context exists, but the exact personal identity and chronology used by the novel were not supported strongly enough by an authoritative one-to-one source.
The reference is legendary/literary; it was not converted into a historical-person record.

The local text does not resolve the individual securely enough for a canonical contextual entity.
These are retained as narrative characters; no historical status was inferred from name or institutional association.
Handled as an active narrative character. The micro-wiki adds the independently sourced Hōzōin-ryū institution rather than merging external biography into his scene record.

book3_exclusions.reason: Mentioned historical roster not promoted in this pass without a sufficiently specific institutional source for every exact identity used by the translation.

entities.name: Kobayakawa Hideaki
entities.summary: Daimyo who defected from the Western Army at Sekigahara and attacked Otani Yoshitsugu's forces, contributing decisively to Tokugawa Ieyasu's victory.

entities.name: Ishida Mitsunari
entities.summary: Toyotomi administrator and principal leader of the Western coalition at Sekigahara, defeated by Tokugawa Ieyasu's coalition.

entities.name: Ukita Hideie
entities.summary: Major Toyotomi ally and commander of a large Western Army contingent at Sekigahara.

entities.name: Shimazu Yoshihiro
entities.summary: Satsuma daimyo and commander of the Shimazu contingent at Sekigahara, later noted for the retreat through the Eastern Army.

entities.name: Konishi Yukinaga
entities.summary: Christian daimyo and Western Army commander at Sekigahara who was captured after the defeat and executed.

entities.name: Tokugawa Ieyasu
entities.summary: Leader of the Eastern Army at Sekigahara whose victory enabled the consolidation of Tokugawa political power.

entities.name: Minamoto no Hiromasa
entities.summary: Heian-period court musician, calligrapher and celebrated flute player, remembered in a medieval anecdote involving a mysterious flute player at Suzaku Gate in Kyoto.

entities.name: Akamatsu clan
entities.summary: A samurai clan based in Harima that became prominent as a shugo-daimyo family during the Muromachi period; Book I connects the Shimmen family to the Akamatsu lineage.

entities.name: Akamatsu Masanori
entities.summary: Akamatsu Masanori was a medieval Japanese military lord and shugo who restored the Akamatsu family's position in Harima, Bizen and Mimasaka during the Muromachi period. Book I invokes him in its account of the Shimmen family's Akamatsu lineage.

entities.name: Battle of Sekigahara
entities.summary: Decisive battle between Tokugawa Ieyasu's Eastern coalition and the Western coalition associated with the Toyotomi cause. The Western defeat transformed the political balance of Japan.

entities.name: Eastern Army
entities.summary: Coalition led by Tokugawa Ieyasu during the Sekigahara campaign of 1600.

entities.name: Western Army
entities.summary: Coalition associated with the Toyotomi cause and commanded at Sekigahara by Ishida Mitsunari and allied daimyo.

entities.name: The Art of War (Sunzi)
entities.period: traditionally attributed to the late 6th–5th century BCE; exact composition date disputed
entities.summary: Ancient Chinese military treatise traditionally attributed to Sunzi (Sun Tzu). Book I invokes it as a model of strategy and military thought, making the work itself part of the historical context rather than a character or faction.

entities.name: Oda Nobunaga
entities.summary: Military leader named in Book II's account of Kyoto's recent political past.

entities.name: Toyotomi Hideyoshi
entities.summary: Ruler and kanpaku named as Nobunaga's successor in Book II's political chronology.

entities.name: Tokugawa Hidetada
entities.summary: Second Tokugawa shogun, named when the novel describes Ieyasu's transfer of the title.

entities.name: Toyotomi Hideyori
entities.summary: Hideyoshi's heir, named at Osaka Castle in Book II's explanation of Tokugawa–Toyotomi tension.

entities.name: Okuni's kabuki-odori
entities.summary: Early-seventeenth-century Kyoto performance tradition associated with Okuni and named as popular entertainment in Book II.
sources: National Theatre of Japan / Japan Arts Council

entities.name: Yagyū Muneyoshi (Sekishūsai)
entities.summary: Historically documented Yagyū master who is first discussed in Book II before becoming an active narrative character.

entities.name: Yagyū Munenori
entities.summary: Sekishūsai's fifth son and later first Yagyū daimyo; Book II reports him away in Edo rather than physically present.

entities.name: Hōzōin-ryū sōjutsu
entities.summary: Spear tradition whose official lineage names Hōzōin Kakuzenbō Hōin In'ei as founder.

entities.name: Kamiizumi Nobutsuna (Lord Ise-no-kami)
entities.summary: Sword master linked with the Yagyū tradition; Book II's translated 'Lord Kōizumi of Ise' is normalized cautiously to this historical context.

entities.name: Fushimi castle town and port
entities.summary: Kyoto City's history describes Fushimi as a road-and-water transport hub shaped by Hideyoshi's castle construction and port development. This supports the broad setting, not the novel's exact worksite.

entities.name: Sasaki Kojirō
entities.summary: The National Diet Library maintains a personal-name authority for Sasaki Kojirō as a swordsman and records 1612 as his death year. The novel's biography, certificate and encounters remain literary evidence.

entities.name: Sumiyoshi Taisha
entities.summary: The shrine's official chronology supports its long historical presence at Sumiyoshi while noting scholarly debate around its traditional foundation date. It does not authenticate the novel's inn or shoreline scenes.

entities.name: Tsukahara Bokuden
entities.summary: Kashima City's cultural-property material identifies Bokuden as a historical swordsman born in 1489 and describes traditions associated with his training. The anecdotes repeated by the novel remain narrative context.

entities.name: Ise Jingū (Naikū)
entities.summary: Official Jingū material identifies Naikū and the Uji Bridge over the Isuzugawa at its entrance. This supports the general geography without fixing narrative scene coordinates.

entities.name: Karasumaru Mitsuhiro
entities.summary: Institutional catalogues identify Karasumaru Mitsuhiro (1579–1638) as a court noble and writer. His role, residence and commissions in the novel are not treated as documentary biography.
sources: Agency for Cultural Affairs / Cultural Heritage Online

entities.name: Great Gojō Bridge
entities.summary: Kyoto City's official chronology records construction of the Great Gojō Bridge in 1589. This supports the bridge's period existence, not the exact position of the novel's posted announcement or encounters.
